description: A global, decentralized information system of documents, applications, and other resources connected through hyperlinks and identified by URIs, accessed over the Internet primarily through HTTP and HTTPS.

source_basis.processing_note: Structured from the supplied article. Relationship edges normalize conceptual links for knowledge-graph use.

definition_and_scope.core_definition: A global interconnected information system that enables content sharing over the Internet using linked resources and Web protocols.
characteristics: Text, images, audio, video, data, and interactive applications

distinctions.Internet: The Internet is the interconnected network infrastructure; the Web is an information system using that infrastructure.
distinctions.website: A website is a collection of related Web resources; the public websites collectively form much of the publicly accessible Web.
distinctions.browser: A browser is client software used to retrieve and render Web resources, not the Web itself.
distinctions.deep_web: Content not indexed by standard search engines; not inherently illicit.
distinctions.dark_web: A distinct category associated with intentionally hidden services and specialized networks; not synonymous with the deep web.

definition_and_scope.license_note: The supplied article says CERN released Web protocols and code royalty-free in April 1993.

history.event: Ted Nelson described a hypertext model linking documents through embedded hotspots.
Tim Berners-Lee developed ENQUIRE at CERN, influencing the Web concept.
Berners-Lee proposed a linked information system to manage and share changing documents and data at CERN.
A working Web system existed, including the WorldWideWeb browser/editor and an HTTP server; early HTTP, URL syntax, and HTML were developed.
The Web was released to research institutions and then made available across the Internet.
Gopher emerged as a menu-oriented information system and early competitor.
CERN made Web protocol and code available royalty-free.
NCSA Mosaic popularized graphical Web browsing, inline images, and forms.
Tim Berners-Lee founded the World Wide Web Consortium to coordinate Web standards.
Pirelli introduced a four-channel wavelength-division multiplexing system, as described in the article.
Netscape Navigator became a major browser; JavaScript was developed for Web pages.
Yahoo! emerged as an early major Web search service.
The Internet Archive began preserving Web pages and historical snapshots.
Google launched as a major Web search engine.
XMLHttpRequest and Ajax-style techniques enabled partial page updates and interactive Web applications.
WHATWG and browser vendors advanced the modern HTML development approach.
The article reports W3C abandoned its XHTML 2.0 effort in favour of the evolving HTML approach.
The article reports W3C ceded control of the HTML specification to WHATWG.

nomenclature.www_prefix_description: A hostname convention, not a technical requirement. It may be used as a subdomain, for DNS aliasing, or for traffic distribution.

layers.name: Internet infrastructure
layers.role: Carries packets between clients and servers.

layers.name: Web application protocols
layers.role: Defines requests, responses, metadata, and secure delivery.

layers.name: Representation
layers.role: Structures and styles content and implements behaviour.

layers.name: Client application
layers.role: Retrieves, interprets, executes, and presents resources.

components.name: Web server
components.role: Receives requests and returns resources, data, or status responses.

components.name: URL
components.role: Locates a resource and describes an access method.

components.name: Domain Name System
components.role: Resolves hostnames and provides related naming records.

steps.name: Navigation
steps.description: A user enters a URL, chooses a bookmark, or follows a link.

steps.name: URL parsing
steps.description: The browser parses scheme, host, path, query, and fragment as applicable.

steps.name: DNS resolution
steps.description: The hostname is resolved to an IP address unless a usable result is already cached or otherwise configured.

steps.name: Connection
steps.description: The client establishes transport and, for HTTPS, TLS security.

steps.name: HTTP request
steps.description: The client sends a method, target, headers, and optional body.

steps.name: Server processing
steps.description: The server routes the request, checks access, reads files or data, and may run application logic.

steps.name: HTTP response
steps.description: The server returns a status code, headers, and optionally a response body.

steps.name: Parsing
steps.description: The browser parses HTML and discovers linked stylesheets, scripts, fonts, images, and media.

steps.name: Subresource retrieval
steps.description: Additional requests fetch resources needed to render and operate the page.

steps.name: Rendering and interaction
steps.description: The browser applies styles, runs permitted scripts, displays content, and handles user input.

example.note: This is a simplified HTTP/1.1 example; modern HTTP versions and caching can alter the actual sequence.

url.purpose: Commonly identifies where and how a resource can be accessed.

hyperlinks.description: Embedded links that let users move between Web resources.

web_graph.directed_edges: Hyperlinks from one resource to another

link_rot.definition: A linked resource disappears, moves, or is replaced, making the original link no longer reach its intended content.

capabilities: References to scripts, stylesheets, fonts, and data

css.purpose: Controls visual presentation, layout, typography, and responsive styling.
css.design_principle: Separates presentation from semantic document structure.

javascript.purpose: Client-side scripting and interactive application behaviour.
javascript.creator: Brendan Eich

web_applications.definition: Web resources that function as application software.

web_page.definition: A document or rendered view suitable for a Web browser.

static_page.definition: A page delivered substantially as stored rather than generated individually for each request.
limitations: Changes require content updates or deployment

dynamic_page.server_side: An application processes requests and constructs or selects a response, often using databases.
dynamic_page.client_side: Browser scripts modify the page through the Document Object Model.

ajax.description: Techniques for retrieving data asynchronously and updating part of a page without a full reload.
ajax.note: Responses need not be XML; JSON is widely used.

website.definition: A collection of related Web resources, commonly grouped under a domain name and published through one or more servers.
website.hosting_note: One server can host multiple sites; a high-traffic site can be served by many servers or a distributed hosting architecture.

browser.definition: A software user agent for retrieving, interpreting, and presenting Web resources.

web_server.definition: Software and execution infrastructure that receives Web requests and serves resources.

web_crawler.definition: An automated client that discovers and fetches Web resources for search, archiving, or analysis.
web_crawler.search_relationship: Search engines commonly crawl, parse, index, and rank accessible content.

internet_and_optical_networking.relationship: The Web depends on Internet connectivity but is a distinct application-layer information system.

optical_networking.definition: Transmission of information over optical fibre using light and optical components.
optical_networking.importance: Fibre infrastructure supports high-volume, long-distance communications among countries, cities, data centres, networks, and residences.

people.name: Pat Nettles
people.role: Ciena chief executive during the described period

people.name: Gordon Gould
people.role: Laser technology figure referenced in the article

people.name: William Culver
people.role: Optical technology figure associated with Optelecom

cookies_and_state.definition: Small pieces of data a website asks a browser to store and return in later requests.

types.name: Session cookie
types.description: Usually associated with a browser session or limited lifetime.

types.name: Persistent cookie
types.description: Stored for a defined period or until deleted.

types.name: First-party cookie
types.description: Set in the context of the site being visited.

types.name: Third-party cookie
types.description: Associated with a different party embedded in or involved in the page context.

types.name: Authentication cookie
types.description: Associates requests with an authenticated session.

types.name: Tracking cookie
types.description: May correlate browsing activity over time or across sites.

security_risks: Cookie exposure through XSS where protections are insufficient
CSRF where application protections are inadequate
cookies_and_state.privacy_note: Consent and disclosure obligations vary by jurisdiction and by storage purpose.

search_engine.definition: Software that searches an information corpus and returns results relevant to a query.

historical_milestones.name: Archie
historical_milestones.description: Early index for FTP archives, not a modern full-text Web search engine.

historical_milestones.name: Yahoo!
historical_milestones.description: Early major Web directory and search service.

historical_milestones.name: Google
historical_milestones.description: Major search engine in large-scale Web search.

deep_web.definition: Web content not indexed by standard search engines.
deep_web.surface_web_distinction: The surface web is the portion discoverable and indexed by ordinary search services under their capabilities and policies.
deep_web.dark_web_distinction: Dark web refers to intentionally hidden services or networks; it is not synonymous with the deep web.

indexing_limits: Dynamic forms and unbounded query spaces

caching.definition: Temporary storage of fetched resources to reduce latency, bandwidth, or repeated processing.

threat_details.name: SQL injection
threat_details.description: Untrusted input changes a database query when applications construct queries unsafely.

threat_details.name: Cross-site scripting
threat_details.description: Attacker-controlled script executes in a victim's browser within a site's security context.
mitigations: Content Security Policy as defence in depth

threat_details.name: Phishing
threat_details.description: Deceptive content attempts to obtain credentials, payment details, or sensitive information.

threat_details.name: Cross-site request forgery
threat_details.description: A victim's browser is induced to make an unintended authenticated request.

threat_details.name: Open redirect
threat_details.description: An unvalidated redirect parameter sends users to an attacker-controlled destination.

https.description: HTTP protected by TLS provides confidentiality and integrity in transit and server authentication when certificate validation succeeds.
limitations: Does not prove content is trustworthy
Does not prevent all endpoint compromise or tracking

defensive_principles: Update browsers, servers, dependencies, and operating systems
Use least privilege and authorization checks
Validate inputs and encode outputs by context
Do not treat historical statistics in the source as current measurements

privacy.private_browsing_caveat: Private or incognito browsing generally limits local persistence on the device; it does not make a user anonymous to websites, network operators, employers, or Internet providers.

standards_and_governance.principle: Interoperable standards allow independently built browsers, servers, and applications to communicate.

organisations.role: Maintains Unicode, foundational for international text.

standards_and_technologies.name: XHTML
standards_and_technologies.role: HTML expressed with XML syntax rules; historical standardization effort

standards_and_governance.governance_note: The Web is decentralized. Standards bodies coordinate specifications, while individuals and organisations operate their own resources.

accessibility.goal: Make Web content usable by people with diverse disabilities, devices, and interaction methods.

internationalisation.goal: Support languages, writing systems, regions, and cultural conventions.

historical_competition.name: Gopher
historical_competition.design: Hierarchical menus pointing to documents and other menus.
historical_competition.contrast: The Web uses hypertext documents that can link freely to other resources.

article_summary.later_outcome: Gopher stagnated and declined while the Web accelerated.

limitations_and_uncertainties: The Web and Internet are distinct even though the Web depends on Internet infrastructure.
Not all Web resources are public or indexed by search engines.
Browser popularity, standards governance, and security statistics can change over time.
Some article content describes historical standards debates rather than the entire current standards landscape.
Graph edges may represent normalized conceptual relationships rather than direct implementation dependencies.
The HTTP example is simplified; modern implementations can differ.
